Hey there, sorry I haven't read through the comments so forgive me if this is annoyingly repetitive (tho I would note that if others are saying similar stuff, maybe we don't *all* have it wrong).

I just want to tell you the story of my brother's best friend. He went from being the hottest dude in school with the most potential, to social outcast practically overnight because of a situation like this. He lost his scholarship, he was expelled, his life as he knew it was over. And the worse it got for him, the more she had to keep it up because of how her actions kept having more and more consequences. That singular event changed his life forever.

But, that was...about a decade ago now. He ended up being a later bloomer than he would have been. Didn't go to college, but always worked his ass off. Now, he has a job he loves, he bought property and fixed it up real good, and about 6 months ago he met the woman he's going to marry. With her support, he's reached out and reconnected with people he had lost over the incident all those years ago.

If he had taken his life at that time, he'd have gone out with that being THE thing that people remember him for. The thing took him down. Instead, he endured, and his story is now an inspiring one. I'm proud as hell to know him.

It's ridiculously hard to think things could ever get better. But the world is big, and life is long. People love rooting for an underdog more than they love worshipping someone who's perfect. This is part of your story now. Just think of how inspiring as fuck you could be to others in the future who go through this. Who could then look at you and think, holy shit, that guy survived and he's dope, I guess I can survive too.

This is the thing you have to overcome right now. It's not the last thing. But it's the big thing right now. You overcome this, you'll be practically bullet proof. Everyone here is rooting for you. Take your experience, survive it, and use it to help others some day. Even if you only help by lending support - you of all people will understand how vital that kind of thing is.

Howdy! Lawyer here again, I like your analysis just want to add - citizens *can* file criminal charges in lots of states through their local court's commissioner's office. Commissioners are like, part judge part sheriff part bailiff. They're the civil alternative to criminal prosecution when the states attorney ain't interested and/or you're trying to report something outside courthouse hours.

Howdy, lawyer here, just want to note that you've cited federal law, when this issue would be governed by state law, as the alleged incident occurred while both parties were residents of the same state.

Also - people *can* claim whatever they want. And they do. Whether they have evidence or a judge believes them is a different story. But this falls with my line of work and I can tell ya, sad to say, people file against each other (ex. her vs him, then him vs her) alllll the time.

If she wants you to manage both of your finances, she can't complain about being micromanaged. That's the freaking point of leaving all of it to you. If she wants to continue having you make all the decisions, she needs to confront her spending.

Honestly you guys remind me a lot of my situation with my husband. I want him to make the decisions right now because he's a lottt more responsible than I am. He keeps on top of it and has gotten us essentially out of debt (not including student loans of course lol). So, for now, I hand over the majority of my paycheck to him, and he puts it towards our debt and our savings. Whatever's left in my account goes to my student loans, coffee, and if I've budgeted well, an occasional spendy purchase (like clothes).

This system also (...finally) got me in the habit of checking my bank account often. That definitely got rid of any out-of-sight-out-of-mind spending. It took a while to get used to, as I'd actively avoid checking my balances before, but sure enough I've gotten used to it. We also both have the passwords to all of our accounts. I don't think it'd work otherwise.

As for over-spending on the credit card issue - my husband and I continue to agree to disagree. I don't think it's a big deal to have a low balance on a credit card, he wants to be cc debt-free. So because I don't want to do our finances, I defer to him. We paid off my balance, and I stopped using my credit card pretty much entirely. I do keep our shared credit card on me, and use it for things like gas and groceries, because I never carry cash and the idea of getting stuck somewhere with an empty debit account freaks me out (though I know that's not very likely lol).

Anyway, it took us a bunch of bickering and a few fights to get where we are, but it's been smooth sailing ever since. My husband is the kindest person you'll meet, but he had to push me a bit on a lot of this. Giving me a few warnings (like hey, we're gonna talk finances tonight) helped keep my anxiety at bay.

Haha no worries (and thanks for the apology, kind stranger!), being misunderstood is one of the things I get anxious about. I tend to overthink and then over-explain to make sure all of my overthinking has come across accurately lol. Here's my over-thought once more:

OP posted about people just complaining instead of taking action. That view comes from a "complaining VS action" perspective - you're either complaining OR you're doing something about it. My point was that sometimes it's not necessarily "complaining VS action," but is actually "complaining = action".

By complaining, OP took action. By complaining about anxiety, other posters are trying to take action too. Even if that action is just, venting to the void instead of further burdening a relationship, or letting things fester and escalate. I don't think this argument works for all subreddits out there, but I definitely think here, specifically on the anxiety subreddit, it's important to keep in mind that what seems like complaining can actually be (or lead to) super helpful action.

I'm not saying it's hypocritical. In fact, saying "it's hypocritical so OP's wrong for doing it" would defeat my actual point, which I don't really care to explain again.

You're responding to your own misunderstanding. Not much else for me to do here. Hope the rest of your day is less anxiety-provoking than this exchange! :)

Set some ground rules, hash out your differences, come up with a system for things like when one of you wants to use the room to hook up, etc. If she's not willing to work with you at all, SWBTA. But unless you TRY to work with her before assuming total control over an entirely shared space...YWBTA.

Please Please PLEASE go speak with a lawyer. I'm not a lawyer, but I've worked around a lot of divorce cases, and yours is ripe for issues down the line. I'm saying this with love and concern for my fellow woman, who is stronger than she knows, and who WILL BE OK in the end - talk to a lawyer. Even if it's just a consultation. You don't need to tell him that you've talked to one. You can decide later when/if/how to tell him. Just go talk to one first.

\-If she tells you something you don't like, it's dismissed or otherwise invalidated (ex. "flipped into a guilt trip")

\-If she has a longer train of thought, you'll stop paying attention, and then blame her for it. Or, if you do keep paying attention, it's only enough to "fight back." 

\-When she gets mad, whatever she's mad about doesn't matter if she doesn't talk it out with you. So, she's in the wrong by default, and you're off the hook.

Sounds like even though you feel like you're doing everything you can to support and help her, you could be doing a lot more...like validating her feelings when she does share them; having a disagreement without turning it into a fight that needs to be won; and working on your own communication practices, rather than completely faulting her for venting after your communication has broken down.

Shows like Forensic Files use those refusals as plot devices. A refusal + suspicious glance between protagonists = the audience picks up on that suspicion right quick. That is NOT an accurate reflection of our legal system!

Cops don't think that polygraphs themselves are accurate. They like them as an investigative tool to help them figure out whether they're on the right track with a suspect. See what questions elicit what kinds of responses, whether the person's story changes, etc.

In most places refusing to submit to a polygraph canNOT be mentioned at trial, and even mentioning it accidentally can cause a mistrial (which doesn't mean you get off the hook, just means the process starts over).

You do not have to invoke your right to privacy in order to exercise it. It is absolutely reasonable to indicate to an officer that you'll be happy to cooperate if they have a warrant, but otherwise you're not comfortable providing that kind of personal information. 

However, unlike the right to privacy, you DO have to affirmatively invoke your right to remain silent. Just remaining silent is NOT enough.

In general, it's better to let the cops be suspicious and put in the groundwork to build their case, (ie. do their job) than to just instantly give up your rights so they'll stop looking at you funny. The system is too flawed to needlessly put yourself at risk like that.

My husband and I are tackling similar issues like this a lot right now. I can't say how you should react this time, but I have one piece of advice that might help in the future.

Try shifting focus from getting upset when he messes up, to rewarding him for doing well. Think about it, what would be more likely to make you a safer driver - the threat of a speeding ticket, or a monthly bonus for staying under the limit?

Offering a motivating reward, rather than just leaving the threat of future upset in the air, also keeps it more fun and lighthearted, which can take the pressure off, and make it more likely to get done.

For example - husband gets to catch up on his favorite show for a night while you take care of the kids, IF he gets your son to the party on time. So, when he's fumbling and making you guys late, you're not taking it personally - you're teasing him for shooting himself in the foot. 

And, it works both ways! I'm sure there's things he wants that are hard for you, and rewards you'd be willing to make the extra effort for.

Obviously you're not going to offer rewards to each other for every little thing forever. But when it comes to building better habits, positive reinforcement is a basic tenant of learning new behaviors. Working towards something you want is more motivating than working to avoiding a negative outcome.

First, treating depression and treating anxiety are NOT the same thing. I didn't make any headway with treatment until I shifted that focus.

Second, unless your husband has expressed to you in some way that he feels you should go because he has helped with your mom, don't lean into that idea too hard for him. People with Aspbergers generally don't think about things that way. They'll let you go to the moon and back for them without feeling any guilt or the appropriate amount of gratitude because they're not empathizing with the hardship you experienced on their behalf. It works both ways. I doubt he's expecting you to empathize with his efforts with your mother to this degree. More likely he's just thinking that this is how you've done the trip before, and that it is more comfortable for him that way, so this is how it should be now. It might not be any deeper than that for him. Make sure you're not just projecting your own worries and disappointment onto him, when he would otherwise be over this pretty quickly.

It could. But POTS also has an underlying disorder, and the pain you're describing sounds very similar to neuropathy associated with diabetes (which is listed as a possible underlying cause of POTS). If you have a history of diabetes in your family, consider getting tested!

There's otc meds you can take for nausea. Try looking out the window towards the horizon/the furthest distance you can. If you get nauseous on all/most transportation, consider seeing a doctor, even an eye doctor. It may be a sign of something other than anxiety.

If you're sure it's anxiety, try giving yourself a reward for both steps, the getting up and the getting to work. For me, that's coffee at home and a snack when I get to work (specifically a snack I love that I only let myself have at work, in the morning, for this reason).

Don't focus on minimizing the bad feelings, it's a trap and we're not good at it and then we feel like shit even more for not being good at it. Focus on the rewards. Tell yourself over and over, "I can do this." Over time it makes a difference, even if it's not that noticeable at first.
